intro: This module prepares an organization for the day something goes wrong. You will build an incident response plan around NIST SP 800-61, test it with tabletop exercises, design backups and disaster recovery that meet stated RTO and RPO targets, run a business impact analysis and plan for ransomware, and validate detections with purple team exercises. Readiness is not a document on a shelf; it is practiced, measured and corrected before a real attacker forces the test.

lessons.title: IR plan and roles
lessons.why: When an incident starts, nobody has time to decide who is in charge; a written, rehearsed plan removes confusion at the worst moment.

p: NIST SP 800-61 Revision 2 describes four phases: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity. The newer Revision 3 aligns incident response with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 functions, but the same ideas remain. An IR plan states the mission, scope, definitions of event versus incident, severity levels, and the authority of the response team to act, including taking systems offline. Executive sign-off matters, because responders will need to make disruptive decisions quickly.

A plan names roles, not only people, because people go on holiday. Typical roles are the incident commander who owns decisions, a technical lead for investigation, a communications lead, a legal and privacy contact, a scribe who keeps the timeline, and liaisons from IT operations, HR and the business. Escalation criteria tie severity to who is notified and how fast: for example a severity 1 incident, such as confirmed data theft, pages the commander within 15 minutes and informs the executive team within an hour. Keep a current contact list with out-of-band methods.

Communication has three audiences: the response team, internal stakeholders and external parties such as customers, regulators, insurers and law enforcement. Assume the corporate chat and email may be compromised, so define a fallback channel. Legal duties differ by region and sector; GDPR requires notifying the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach where required, and many contracts set shorter windows. Route outside statements through one approved spokesperson and use templates prepared in advance.

Beneath the plan sit playbooks for common scenarios such as ransomware, business email compromise, lost laptop and web application compromise. Each lists triggers, first actions, decision points and who to call. Prepare a jump kit: forensic tools, clean workstations, write blockers, access to logs and a documented chain of custody process so evidence stays usable. Review the plan at least yearly and after every incident or major infrastructure change, and keep a printed or offline copy for when systems are unavailable.

snippet.label: Plan excerpt
snippet.text:
Severity 1: confirmed data loss or active ransomware
  Notify: Incident Commander within 15 min
  Notify: CISO, Legal within 60 min
  Decision rights: IC may isolate any system
  Backup channel: phone bridge 555-0100 (fictional)
  Regulatory clock: privacy officer assesses 72h duty

lessons.example: A fictional company, Example Corp, detects encrypted files on a file server at 02:10. The on-call analyst declares severity 1 under the plan, which automatically pages the incident commander. The commander opens the phone bridge because email is suspect, assigns a scribe, tasks IT to isolate the file server's VLAN, and asks legal to start the 72 hour breach assessment clock. Because roles, thresholds and contact details were already written down, the first hour is spent acting, not arguing.

terms.def: The person with overall authority for decisions during an incident.
A classification that determines urgency, escalation and notification.
A scenario specific checklist of response actions.
Documentation of who handled evidence and when.
A communication path independent of the possibly compromised network.

check.q: Which are the four NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2 phases?
options: Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity
check.why: That is the Rev 2 lifecycle.

check.q: Why define roles rather than names?
check.why: Roles can be filled by deputies.

check.q: Why a backup communications channel?
check.why: Attackers may read corporate chat or email.

check.q: The scribe's job is to...
options: Keep the timeline of events and decisions
check.why: A timeline supports analysis and later review.

recap: Follow the NIST lifecycle and get executive authority in writing.
Define roles, severity levels, escalation and contact paths.
Keep scenario playbooks, an evidence process and an offline plan copy.

lessons.title: Tabletop exercises
lessons.why: A plan only proves its worth when people rehearse it; tabletops expose gaps cheaply, without risking production.

p: A tabletop exercise is a facilitated discussion in which participants walk through a realistic scenario and describe what they would do. No systems are touched. It differs from a full simulation or a technical red team test, and it is the cheapest way to test decisions, roles, communication and the plan itself. Include not only security staff but also IT operations, legal, communications, HR, a business owner and an executive sponsor, because most real incident delays come from decisions, approvals and handoffs rather than from technology.

Start with an objective, such as testing the ransomware playbook or the breach notification decision. Write a believable scenario drawn from your threat landscape, then script injects, the new pieces of information fed in at timed intervals: 'Backups appear to be encrypted', 'A journalist emails asking about a leak', 'The attacker posts sample data'. Good injects force trade-offs, create time pressure and introduce ambiguity. Prepare facilitator notes with expected actions, so the discussion can be compared against the plan, and keep the scenario fictional or anonymized.

A facilitator keeps time, reads injects, asks open questions such as 'who decides that, and how do you reach them at 3 a.m.?' and stops arguments that drift into blame. An observer records decisions, delays and assumptions. Sessions typically last two to three hours. Use a no-fault rule: the purpose is to find weaknesses in the process, and people who admit they do not know something are helping. Rotate scenarios so different teams and plans, including cloud and third-party failures, are tested over the year.

Immediately after, hold a hot wash to gather impressions, then write a short report listing findings, evidence from the notes, a severity, a named owner and a due date. Track actions in the same ticket system used for engineering work and review them at a regular meeting until closed. Examples include an outdated contact list, no authority to shut down a production line, or no template for customer notice. Measure improvement by repeating a similar scenario later and checking that earlier gaps no longer appear.

snippet.label: Inject card
snippet.text:
T+00 Alert: file server shows .locked extensions
T+20 Inject: backups console unreachable
T+45 Inject: ransom note demands payment, 72h deadline
T+70 Inject: customer asks if their data is affected
Questions: who isolates? who informs legal? who speaks?

lessons.example: During a tabletop, the group reaches the inject about customer data and discovers nobody knows who may approve a public statement. The legal lead assumes communications decides, while communications assumes the CEO decides. The observer records a gap titled 'No approval path for external statements', assigns it to the communications director, and sets a due date four weeks out. At the next quarterly exercise the group checks that a one page approval flow exists and that it works.

terms.def: A scripted piece of new information introduced during an exercise.
A quick debrief right after an exercise.
The person who guides the exercise and keeps it on track.
A ground rule that the exercise tests process, not individuals.
A tracked task with an owner and due date that closes a gap.

check.q: What is an inject?
options: New information fed during the exercise
check.why: Injects drive the scenario forward.

check.q: A tabletop primarily tests...
check.why: It is a discussion based exercise.

check.q: Why include legal and communications?
options: Many incident delays involve decisions and notices
check.why: Incidents are business events, not only technical.

check.q: Best way to treat findings?
check.why: Tracked actions get closed.

recap: Tabletops are low cost discussions that test the plan.
Use timed injects, mixed participants and a no-fault rule.
Record gaps as owned, dated actions and re-test later.

lessons.title: Backups and disaster recovery
lessons.why: Backups are the last line of defense against ransomware and failure, but only if they are intact, isolated and proven to restore.

p: The classic 3-2-1 rule says keep three copies of data, on two different media types, with one copy off site. The modern extension 3-2-1-1-0 adds one copy that is offline, air-gapped or immutable, and zero errors after verification. Immutable storage uses write once, read many features such as object lock in compliance mode, so even an administrator with stolen credentials cannot delete or encrypt backups before the retention period ends. Separate backup credentials from the domain, and require multi person approval to change retention.

Two numbers drive design. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum tolerable data loss measured in time: an RPO of one hour means backups or replication must occur at least hourly. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum tolerable time to restore service: an RTO of four hours means the restore process, bandwidth and staffing must be capable of that. Tighter targets cost more, for example continuous replication versus nightly backup, so business owners should set them based on the cost of downtime and data loss.

A full backup copies everything; an incremental copies changes since the last backup of any type; a differential copies changes since the last full. Incrementals are small and fast to take but need the chain to restore, while differentials restore with two sets. Snapshots are quick but usually live on the same storage and do not replace backups. Retention should cover both operational needs and hidden compromise: if an attacker lived in the network for 60 days, you may need clean restore points older than that. Encrypt backups and protect the keys separately.

A backup that has never been restored is only a hope. Schedule restore tests, automate integrity checks, and time a full recovery of a critical system against its RTO. Disaster recovery sites come as hot (running, near instant failover), warm (partly provisioned) or cold (space and hardware only), trading cost against recovery time. In the cloud, use separate accounts and regions for copies, and document runbooks so that recovery does not depend on the knowledge of one person. Record every test result and fix failures.

snippet.label: Backup policy
snippet.text:
dataset: erp-db
rpo: 1h        rto: 4h
schedule: full weekly, incremental hourly
copies: 3  media: disk + object storage
offsite: region-b   immutable: 35 days (object lock)
restore_test: monthly, result logged

lessons.example: A finance database must lose no more than one hour of data and be back within four hours. The team takes hourly incrementals with a weekly full, keeps a copy in another region with object lock for 35 days, and tests restores monthly. A drill shows the restore takes six hours because of slow transfer. That exceeds the RTO, so they stage the latest full backup in the recovery region and retest, bringing the time to three and a half hours.

terms.def: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time.
The maximum acceptable time to restore a service.
A copy that cannot be altered or deleted until retention expires.
Isolation of a copy from the network.
A fully equipped recovery site that can take over almost immediately.

check.q: What does the final 0 in 3-2-1-1-0 mean?
check.why: Backups are verified, with no errors.

check.q: An RPO of 1 hour means...
options: At most 1 hour of data loss is tolerable
check.why: RPO measures data loss.

check.q: Why are snapshots on the same array not enough?
options: They share the failure and attack domain
check.why: If storage or credentials fall, snapshots go too.

check.q: What proves a backup is usable?
check.why: Only restore testing proves recoverability.

recap: Follow 3-2-1-1-0 with an immutable or offline copy.
Set RPO and RTO with the business and design to meet them.
Test restores on a schedule and keep recovery runbooks.

lessons.title: Business continuity and ransomware resilience
lessons.why: Recovery is not only about restoring files; it is about restoring the right systems, in the right order, while the business keeps functioning.

p: A business impact analysis (BIA) identifies critical business processes and measures the effect of their interruption over time: lost revenue, regulatory penalties, safety impacts and reputational harm. From it you derive the maximum tolerable downtime, then an RTO and RPO for each process and supporting system. Interview process owners, not only IT, because the people who run payroll or order fulfilment know what breaks first. Rank services into tiers, such as tier 0 for identity and networking, tier 1 for revenue systems and tier 2 for internal tools.

Systems depend on others, and recovery must follow that graph. Almost everything needs identity services (Active Directory or an identity provider), DNS, DHCP, networking and time before applications can work, so those come first. Next are databases and storage, then application servers, then front ends, then user facing integrations. Map third-party dependencies such as payment providers and SaaS. Record the order in a recovery runbook with owners and estimated times, and note any circular dependency, for example a backup system that needs the very directory it must restore.

Modern ransomware often combines data theft with encryption, so recovery from backup solves only part of the problem; you may still face extortion and notification duties. Plan for loss of the domain, hypervisors and backup consoles at once. Prepare an isolated clean room to rebuild and scan restored systems before reconnecting, and keep offline copies of golden images, configurations and the runbook itself. Decide in advance who may authorize negotiations or payment, and consult legal counsel and law enforcement guidance, since sanctions and policy considerations apply.

Business continuity plans cover people, premises, process and technology: manual workarounds such as paper forms, alternative offices, a staff call tree and priority customer communication. Define the threshold for declaring a disaster and activating the plan. Exercise it with both tabletop and technical recovery tests, and update it when systems change. Cyber insurance may require specific controls and prompt notice, so know the policy requirements ahead of time. Success means critical services return within tolerance, not that every server is restored.

snippet.label: BIA table
snippet.text:
Process        MTD   RTO   RPO   Depends on
Payroll        72h   24h   4h    AD, DB, HR app
Online orders  4h    2h    15m   DNS, DB, API, payments
Intranet       7d    3d    24h   AD, web server
Tier order: identity/DNS -> databases -> apps -> front ends

lessons.example: After a fictional ransomware attack, Example Corp finds the domain controllers encrypted. The runbook says identity comes first, so the team restores an offline copy of a domain controller into the clean room, validates it, and brings up DNS. Only then are the order database, API servers and payment integration restored, matching the BIA tiers. Online ordering resumes in six hours, inside its tolerance of eight, while the intranet waits two days, exactly as the business had agreed beforehand.

terms.def: An analysis of how interruptions to business processes affect the organization over time.
Maximum tolerable downtime before the impact becomes unacceptable.
A ranking that sets restoration priority.
An isolated environment used to rebuild and inspect systems safely.
Ransomware that both encrypts and steals data for leverage.

check.q: What does a BIA produce?
check.why: It sets priorities and tolerances.

check.q: Which is usually restored first?
check.why: Most services depend on them.

check.q: Why is restoring from backup alone not enough against double extortion?
options: Data may also have been stolen
check.why: Stolen data creates extortion and notification duties.

check.q: Why include process owners in a BIA?
options: They know business impact and workarounds
check.why: IT alone cannot judge business impact.

recap: Run a BIA to set tiers, RTO and RPO per process.
Map dependencies and restore identity and networking first.
Plan for ransomware with a clean room and offline runbooks.

lessons.title: Purple team exercises
lessons.why: Purple teaming joins attackers and defenders to measure which behaviors your controls actually detect, then fixes the gaps on the spot.

p: A red team emulates an adversary, a blue team defends and detects, and a purple team exercise has both work together in real time rather than in secret. The red side runs a technique, the blue side checks whether the right telemetry and alert appeared, and together they tune until it does. The goal is not to win but to improve detection coverage. This is far faster than a classic red team engagement, where findings arrive in a report weeks later.

sections.h: MITRE ATT&CK and Atomic Red Team
p: MITRE ATT&CK is a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques, each with an ID such as T1059.001 (PowerShell) or T1003.001 (LSASS memory credential dumping). Atomic Red Team is an open library of small, scripted tests mapped to those technique IDs, designed to run safely on a lab system so defenders can verify detection. Invoke-AtomicTest T1059.001 runs the tests for that technique, and a cleanup step reverses changes. Always run tests only on authorized lab or test systems, with written approval and rollback.

Choose techniques based on threat intelligence about groups that target your sector, and agree scope and safety rules. For each test, record the time and expected data source, execute it, and look in the SIEM or EDR. Classify the outcome: logged and alerted, logged but no alert, or no telemetry. Each result suggests a fix: enable a missing log source such as Sysmon or PowerShell script block logging, write a detection rule, or adjust response. Re-run the same test to confirm the new rule fires.

Track detection coverage as a share of tested techniques with working alerts, mean time to detect for the simulated activity, and the false positive rate of new rules. Store rules and test mappings in version control and replay the tests automatically after changes so that detections do not quietly break, a practice often called detection as code. Rotate through ATT&CK tactics over the year, and feed lessons into the IR plan and tabletop scenarios. A single run is a snapshot; regular repetition builds confidence.

snippet.label: Test and result
snippet.text:
> Invoke-AtomicTest T1059.001 -TestNumbers 1   (lab host ws-lab01)
12:04:10 executed, encoded PowerShell command
SIEM: event 4104 present, rule 'Suspicious PowerShell' = no alert
Gap: logged but not alerted
Fix: add rule for -EncodedCommand with long base64
12:41:55 re-run -> alert fired

lessons.example: A purple team picks T1059.001 because a fictional threat group relevant to Example Corp uses encoded PowerShell. The red operator runs an Atomic test on a lab host, and the blue analyst sees script block event 4104 in the SIEM but no alert. Together they write a rule that matches long encoded commands from non-admin parent processes, test it against 24 hours of benign data to keep false positives low, deploy it, and re-run the test. The alert fires, and the coverage chart improves by one technique.

terms.def: A collaborative exercise where attack emulation and defense tune detections together.
A knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques.
A library of small tests mapped to ATT&CK techniques.
An attack behavior that produces no useful alert.
Managing detection rules and tests in version control with automated checks.

check.q: What distinguishes purple from classic red teaming?
options: Attackers and defenders collaborate in real time
check.why: Immediate feedback speeds tuning.

check.q: What is a technique ID like T1003.001?
check.why: ATT&CK uses T-prefixed IDs.

check.q: Logged but not alerted means...
options: Telemetry exists, a rule is missing
check.why: The fix is a detection rule.

check.q: Where may Atomic tests be run?
check.why: They simulate real behavior and need approval.

recap: Purple teams test and tune detections together.
Map tests to ATT&CK and classify results as alerted, logged or blind.
Fix gaps, re-run to confirm and automate replay.

labs.title: Tabletop a ransomware case
labs.scenario: Example Corp, a fictional firm, faces a ransomware outbreak. You are the incident commander and will receive timed injects. At each step you must decide on containment, communication and recovery, balancing business impact against risk. The plan names a legal lead and a communications lead, and backups are in an unknown state.
labs.objective: Make sound containment, communication and recovery decisions across timed injects.

steps.do: Inject T+00: file server shows .locked extensions. Choose an action.
steps.see: Options: isolate VLAN, power off, ignore. You choose isolate VLAN. Feedback: good, preserves memory and stops spread.

steps.do: Inject T+20: backup console is unreachable. Choose.
steps.see: Options: assume backups fine, check immutable copy, rebuild blindly. You check the immutable copy. Feedback: object lock copy verified from 03:00.

steps.do: Inject T+45: ransom note with a 72 hour deadline. Choose who to notify.
steps.see: Choose legal, CISO and insurer. Feedback: correct, regulatory clock and policy notice start.

steps.do: Inject T+70: customer asks if their data is affected. Choose a response.
steps.see: Options: deny, say nothing, holding statement approved by legal. You choose the holding statement. Feedback: correct.

steps.do: Inject T+120: attacker posts sample data online. Choose.
steps.see: Confirm data theft; privacy officer starts breach assessment. Feedback: recovery alone does not close the incident.

steps.do: Choose the recovery order.
steps.see: Identity, DNS, databases, apps. Feedback: matches BIA tiers. Score: 5 of 5 decisions on plan.

labs.answer: Best decisions: isolate the affected VLAN, verify the immutable backups, notify legal, the CISO and the insurer, send an approved holding statement, treat the data posting as a breach, and restore identity and DNS before applications.
labs.hint: Think containment first, evidence second, communications through one approved voice.

labs.title: Pick backup strategy
labs.scenario: A logistics company needs its order database to meet an RPO of 30 minutes and an RTO of 4 hours, and must survive ransomware that steals admin credentials. You edit a backup configuration for schedule, retention, immutability and testing.
labs.objective: Configure backups that meet the stated RPO and RTO and resist credential theft.

steps.do: Open backup.yaml
steps.see: Fields: schedule, retention_days, immutable, offsite, restore_test. Current: daily full, 7 days, immutable false.

steps.do: Set schedule to incremental every 15 minutes plus nightly full
steps.see: Validator: RPO 15m satisfies target 30m

steps.do: Set offsite to true with a second region
steps.see: Validator: copy count 3, offsite present

steps.do: Set immutable true, 35 days, compliance mode
steps.see: Validator: deletion blocked until expiry, ransomware resistant

steps.do: Set restore_test to monthly full restore with timing
steps.see: Validator: expected restore 3h10m, under RTO 4h

steps.do: Save and run validation
steps.see: All checks passed: RPO ok, RTO ok, immutability ok

labs.answer: Use 15 minute incrementals with a nightly full, an off-site copy in another region, 35 day immutable retention in compliance mode, and monthly timed restore tests showing recovery under 4 hours.
labs.hint: The schedule interval must be no longer than the RPO, and immutability defeats stolen credentials.

labs.title: Recovery order
labs.scenario: After a BIA at Example Corp, you must sequence the restoration of seven systems following a ransomware event: identity service, DNS and DHCP, order database, payment gateway, web front end, payroll app and intranet. Drag them into the correct order on the dependency diagram.
labs.objective: Sequence recovery by dependency and business criticality.

steps.do: Drag Identity service to position 1
steps.see: Accepted: no dependencies

steps.do: Drag DNS and DHCP to position 2
steps.see: Accepted: needs network only

steps.do: Drag Order database to position 3
steps.see: Accepted: depends on identity and DNS

steps.do: Drag Payment gateway to position 4
steps.see: Accepted: depends on database

steps.do: Drag Web front end to position 5
steps.see: Accepted: depends on API and payments

steps.do: Place Payroll app then Intranet last
steps.see: Accepted: lower tiers. Validation passed: all dependencies satisfied before each step

labs.answer: Correct order: identity service, DNS and DHCP, order database, payment gateway, web front end, payroll app, intranet. Foundational services precede dependent ones, and higher tier revenue systems precede internal tools.
labs.hint: Restore what everything else depends on before the applications.

labs.title: Purple team detection gap
labs.scenario: In a lab, the red operator will run an Atomic Red Team test for T1059.001 (encoded PowerShell) on host ws-lab01. You monitor the SIEM and must determine whether the technique is detected and, if not, write the missing rule.
labs.objective: Find the undetected technique and create a detection that fires on re-test.

steps.do: Start the simulated technique
steps.see: Red: executed T1059.001 test 1 at 12:04:10

steps.do: Search SIEM: host=ws-lab01 earliest=-15m
steps.see: 3 events: process create, event 4104 script block, network connect

steps.do: Check alerts for the same window
steps.see: 0 alerts. Coverage: T1059.001 = not detected

steps.do: Open event 4104 and note fields
steps.see: Fields: ScriptBlockText, powershell.exe -EncodedCommand JAB..., ParentImage winword.exe

steps.do: Write rule: powershell with -EncodedCommand, base64 length over 100, parent not an admin tool
steps.see: Rule saved; backtest on 24h: 0 false positives

steps.do: Ask red to re-run the test
steps.see: Alert fired: Suspicious Encoded PowerShell, ws-lab01, 12:41:55

labs.answer: The technique was logged (event 4104) but not alerted. The fix is a rule on encoded PowerShell with long base64 content and an unusual parent process, validated by a backtest and a re-run that produced an alert.
labs.hint: Telemetry existed, so the gap is a rule, not a log source.

options: Findings with owners and due dates
An offline or immutable copy and zero verification errors
checkpoint.why: The extra 1 is offline or immutable, 0 is errors.

options: Service must be restored within 4 hours

checkpoint.why: It ranks processes and sets tolerances.
